clinicalPearls: Classic mpox/smallpox prodrome: fever first, followed days later by rash; other prodromal features include malaise, sore throat, and headache (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Lymphadenopathy is a key historical feature distinguishing mpox (present) from smallpox (absent) in endemic countries (Harrison 22e p.1519).

Classic systemic orthopoxvirus rash evolves through macular, papular, vesicular, and pustular phases (the pustular stage with central umbilication), each stage lasting 2-3 days, with lesions in the same anatomic location typically at the same stage of development (Harrison 22e p.1519).

Classic distribution is diffuse, well-circumscribed, and centrifugal: lesions more prominent on face and extremities (including palms and soles) than on the trunk; lesions are painful as they emerge and become pruritic in later stages (Harrison 22e p.1519).

In the 2022 clade IIb outbreak, transmission was primarily through close, intimate (e.g., sexual) contact and predominantly affected gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (MSM) (Harrison 22e p.1518).

Clade IIb mpox often departed from the classic picture: rash was frequently the first or only sign (prodrome absent or concurrent), lesions were often localized to the anogenital region, smaller, fewer (often <10), and could be at different stages at the same anatomic site (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Up to 50% of those diagnosed during the 2022 outbreak in the U.S. context were also living with HIV (Harrison 22e p.1518).

Molluscum contagiosum (MCV) has a classic pearly appearance that may umbilicate as it matures, with little surrounding inflammation and painless lesions that persist for months but gradually regress over 6-12 months (Harrison 22e p.1519).

The infectious period for orthopoxvirus infections lasts from symptom onset until all lesions have crusted, the crusts have separated, and fresh healthy skin has formed underneath; lesion scabs contain viable virus (Harrison 22e p.1518).

Two distinct MPXV clades exist: Clade I (formerly Congo Basin, Central Africa) causes a higher proportion of severe disease than Clade II (formerly West African); Clade II subdivides into IIa (endemic West Africa) and IIb (spread worldwide in 2022) (Harrison 22e p.1517).
harrison.pathophysiology: Poxviruses are large double-stranded DNA viruses that replicate entirely in the cytoplasm. Orthopoxvirus infection (variola, MPXV) is thought to involve systemic spread from the inoculation site to local lymph nodes, seeding of lymphoreticular tissue, and then symptomatic (febrile) viremia with viral skin tropism; disease severity reflects how well innate immune and interferon responses control early infection. Immunocompetent hosts develop lesions (often at the exposure site) about 1 week after exposure, progressing through staged phases over 7-14 days with scabbing and resolution by 14-21 days after rash onset. In severe immunocompromise (e.g., advanced HIV with CD4 <200 cells/mm3, organ transplantation), MPXV spread/growth goes unchecked, producing wide dissemination with large confluent lesions persisting for months and additional organ involvement. Most other poxvirus infections (e.g., parapoxviruses, MCV) involve only local viral growth at the inoculation site; yatapoxvirus (tanapox) pathogenesis is poorly understood (Harrison 22e p.1518).
additionalDifferentials: Syphilis (anogenital mpox lesions may resemble STIs) (Harrison 22e p.1519)
Cutaneous anthrax (particularly with parapoxvirus infections) (Harrison 22e p.1519)
Smallpox (variola) - distinguished from mpox classically by absence of lymphadenopathy (Harrison 22e p.1519)
infectionMimics: Syphilis and other STIs (gonorrhea, chlamydia) in anogenital presentations (Harrison 22e p.1519)
Malaria (tanapox initially presents with very high fever and may be mistaken for malaria in endemic areas) (Harrison 22e p.1519)
additionalInvestigations: Nucleic acid (molecular) testing is the most common diagnostic tool: PCR assays for non-variola orthopoxvirus (NVO), orthopoxvirus generic, generic mpox, and mpox clade II; sequencing for full isolate characterization (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Multiplex assays combining NVO- and MPXV-specific targets, and clade-specific testing (U.S. Government and Public Health Laboratories), are available (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Viral culture: orthopoxviruses grow well in standard clinical tissue culture; parapoxviruses are difficult to isolate (primary cells best); MCV cannot be cultured (Harrison 22e p.1519).

Electron microscopy: characteristic large brick-shaped particles on negative stain for orthopoxvirus, yatapoxvirus, or MCV; parapoxviruses show an ovoid structure with crisscross spicules (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Histopathology of biopsy: MCV shows classic Henderson-Patterson bodies (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Serology can demonstrate orthopoxvirus reactivity but most assays cannot distinguish between orthopoxvirus species due to broad antigenic similarity (Harrison 22e p.1519).
redFlags: Severe immunocompromise (advanced HIV with CD4 <200 cells/mm3, especially <50; organ transplantation) predisposes to severe, disseminated, prolonged mpox with numerous large coalescing or necrotic lesions and multi-organ involvement (GI tract, liver, lungs, brain) (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Ocular involvement: eye pain, redness, vision changes/loss, periorbital swelling, blepharitis, conjunctivitis, keratitis - can result in vision loss (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Neurologic complications: encephalitis, myelitis - severe headache, neck pain, altered mentation, focal deficits (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Myopericarditis: dyspnea or palpitations with elevated cardiac biomarkers and ECG changes (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Mucosal complications affecting alimentation, urination, or defecation due to painful or obstructive lesions; may lead to strictures, edema, and severe lymphadenopathy (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Most deaths have occurred predominantly among people with advanced HIV and CD4 <50 cells/mm3 (Harrison 22e p.1519).
harrison.prognosis: In immunocompetent hosts most poxvirus infections are self-limited, resolving in weeks (or months for molluscum contagiosum). Exceptions are the generalized orthopoxvirus infections caused by MPXV and variola, which carry higher case-fatality. In unvaccinated individuals smallpox mortality is up to 30%; MPXV mortality is approximately 1.4-10% (clade I), ~1% (clade IIa), and <1% (clade IIb). Immunocompromised hosts may have more severe orthopoxvirus and parapoxvirus disease (severe mpox, progressive vaccinia, eczema vaccinatum, severe borealpox) with higher mortality, or atypical presentations (e.g., giant orf). In advanced HIV, effective antiretroviral therapy is essential to favorable outcomes. MCV can be diffuse in the immunocompromised, and immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) has been associated with recrudescence of MCV. Poxvirus reinfections are seldom reported (Harrison 22e p.1521).
pitfalls: Do not assume a classic systemic presentation: during the 2022 clade IIb outbreak rash was often the first/only sign with prodrome absent, lesions localized to the anogenital area, smaller, fewer (<10), and could be at different stages at the same site - contrary to the classic rule that lesions in the same location are at the same stage (Harrison 22e p.1519).

Anogenital mpox lesions can be mistaken for common STIs (gonorrhea, chlamydia, syphilis); up to 10% of mpox patients may be coinfected with an STI, so a positive STI test does not exclude mpox (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Characteristic lesions plus exposure history narrow the differential, but laboratory testing is required to confirm the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Distinguish mpox from varicella (VZV), herpes simplex, and syphilis - overlapping vesiculopustular/anogenital presentations are a recognized diagnostic trap (Harrison 22e p.1519).
MCV cannot be cultured, so reliance on culture for diagnosis of molluscum is futile; biopsy (Henderson-Patterson bodies) or clinical/EM findings are needed (Harrison 22e p.1519).
harrison.severityClassification: Mpox ranges from typical self-limited disease (immunocompetent, including HIV with CD4 >200 cells/mm3, generally without increased severity) to severe mpox. Severe manifestations include ocular infection, neurologic complications (encephalitis, myelitis), myopericarditis, obstructive mucosal disease, and uncontrolled viral replication with disseminated/necrotic lesions and multi-organ involvement, occurring chiefly in severely immunocompromised patients (advanced HIV, organ transplantation). Clade I causes a higher proportion of severe disease than clade II (Harrison 22e p.1519).
management: Supportive care is the mainstay for most immunocompetent cases, with analgesia, skin and wound care, hydration and management of painful proctitis or pharyngitis
Antiviral therapy for severe disease or those at high risk, with tecovirimat as the usual first choice and cidofovir, brincidofovir or vaccinia immune globulin as alternatives
Isolation and infection-control precautions until lesions have crusted and re-epithelialised, together with contact tracing
Pre-exposure and post-exposure vaccination of contacts and at-risk groups with a modified vaccinia Ankara vaccine
Test for and manage co-infections including HIV and other sexually transmitted infections, optimising antiretroviral therapy in advanced HIV given the risk of unchecked dissemination
Monitor for and escalate complications such as secondary bacterial infection, ocular involvement, encephalitis and dehydration, hospitalising severe or immunocompromised patients
